sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Agrarian Base**: The economy was primarily agrarian, with the state claiming a significant share of the produce, often collected through the **Tarafdari system**.
• **Trade Dynamics**: The Bahmanis controlled key ports like **Dabhol and Chaul**, facilitating trade with the Middle East and Europe, primarily in horses and textiles.
• **Currency System**: The Bahmani Sultans issued gold (**Huns**) and copper coins, reflecting a monetized economy in urban centers.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: The **'Taraf'** (province) served as the primary unit for revenue collection, managed by a **Tarafdar** (Governor) who maintained troops for the Sultan.

items.definition: Administrative division of the kingdom into four provinces (Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Bidar, Berar). Governors (Tarafdars) collected revenue and maintained the army.
Gold currency used in the Bahmani kingdom, showing the influence of the earlier Yadava and later Vijayanagara monetary standards.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Military-Fiscal Linkage**: The economy was geared toward sustaining a large standing army to counter the Vijayanagara Empire.
• **Urbanization**: Growth of capital cities like Gulbarga and Bidar as centers of craft production and trade.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Key Challenges**: Constant warfare drained the treasury; regional autonomy of Tarafdars led to decentralization.
• **Solutions**: Administrative reforms by Mahmud Gawan to centralize revenue collection and limit the power of provincial governors.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'G-D-B-B' (The 4 Provinces: Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Bidar, Berar).
• **Decoded Meaning**: These were the four original Tarafs established by Muhammad Shah I.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: Do not confuse the Bahmani 'Tarafdari' system with the Mughal 'Mansabdari' system. While similar in military obligation, the Bahmani system was more decentralized and prone to provincial rebellion.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Military-Fiscalism' to describe the Bahmani state, where the entire economic apparatus was subservient to the requirements of the military machine.

keyTakeaways: The Bahmani economy was a classic example of a military-fiscal state in the Deccan.
Control over Konkan ports was the primary driver of external trade and wealth.
Mahmud Gawan's reforms were the most significant attempt to centralize the agrarian economy.
